title: The Inventory of the coast road
premise: Yara Amberdale has spent a decade writing postcards to her family's burned-down coastal house, unsent confessions addressed to the sister who died in the fire she may have caused. When Meriel Kestrel, the last fluent speaker of a dying local tongue, asks Yara to become her final student, the lessons force Yara to learn words for things English let her avoid: blame, debt, forgiveness. As the estate sale of the ruined house approaches and Meriel's health fails, Yara discovers her estranged brother Teo has returned to buy the land — and that Meriel was the one who pulled them both from the fire years ago. In the novel's final movement, Yara must speak the truth aloud in a language only two people will ever fully share, choosing confession over the comfortable silence her whole family arranged itself around.
about_author: Emrys Zhou is the pen name of a former archivist who spent seven years cataloguing endangered-language recordings along the northern coast before turning to fiction. Their work explores how families survive their own histories, and what gets lost in translation between silence and speech.

chapters.title: Postcards to Ash
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. We meet her ritual: weekly postcards to an address that no longer exists, each one almost saying something. She works at a stationery shop, lives small, avoids the coast road. Emotional beat: the ache of practiced avoidance, and the first crack — a postcard she can't bring herself to write at all.

chapters.title: The Last Speaker
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Meriel Kestrel appears at the shop, having traced Yara through a newspaper feature on letter-writers. She offers to teach Yara Kerowen, the language of the cove where Yara grew up, before it dies with her. Yara refuses twice; the third time, Meriel says something in Kerowen that sounds like her dead sister's nickname. Beat: dread disguised as curiosity.

chapters.title: First Words
chapters.summary: Yara's POV, interspersed with lesson transcripts. Early lessons: Meriel teaches nouns for weather, tide, grief. Yara learns the language has no word for 'accident' — only words distinguishing 'did' from 'let happen.' The distinction lands like a blow. Beat: the past becoming grammatically unavoidable.

chapters.title: The Brother Returns
chapters.summary: Teo's POV. He arrives in town to bid on the house sale, telling himself he's after the land value, not closure. He sees Yara leaving Meriel's cottage and doesn't approach. Flashback fragments: the night of the fire, a door he couldn't open. Beat: guilt wearing the costume of practicality.

chapters.title: What the Tide Keeps
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Meriel reveals she was the volunteer who pulled both children from the burning house — and that Yara's mother begged her afterward never to say what she saw. Meriel has kept the secret ten years but is dying, and secrets are heavy luggage. Beat: betrayal braided with tenderness; Yara flees mid-lesson.

chapters.title: Auction Notice
chapters.summary: Alternating Yara and Teo POVs. The sale date is set; siblings circle each other at the town's one café, speaking in logistics instead of truth. Teo learns Yara has been sending postcards all these years and realizes he wasn't the only one who never left. Beat: two people orbiting the same wound without touching it.

chapters.title: The Grammar of Blame
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Reconciliation with Meriel through study: Yara learns the Kerowen verb forms for responsibility across time, and finally writes a postcard that says too much — then burns it herself. Meriel tells her the fire started from a lamp Yara knocked over fleeing a fight between her parents. Beat: the terrible relief of a fact, which is not yet forgiveness.

chapters.title: Everything the Family Arranged
chapters.summary: Teo's POV. Teo confronts his father, now in a care home, and learns the family's silence was engineered: his mother made everyone promise, believing protection required erasure. Teo realizes buying the house would complete the erasure. Beat: rising tension — the sale closing in days, the truth still unspoken between siblings.

chapters.title: The Question
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. On the eve of the auction, Yara goes to the ruin itself and finds Teo there. In broken Kerowen — the language only she and Meriel now share — she asks him the question the family arranged itself around: whether he blames her. His answer, in English, is that he stopped blaming her the day he realized she'd been blaming herself enough for both of them. Beat: climax; confession met not with absolution but with recognition.

chapters.title: Inventory
chapters.summary: Yara's POV, closing with Meriel's deathbed scene. The siblings withdraw from the sale together and instead donate the land as a Kerowen place-name reserve. At Meriel's bedside, Yara speaks a full sentence in Kerowen — a promise to keep the language, and the truth, alive. Final image: a postcard, addressed and stamped, mailed at last to Teo's new address. Beat: quiet resolution; survival priced honestly, and paid.
